claims.text: Under rapid heating and cooling, single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticle formation is governed by suppression of atomic mobility.
An extremely brief high-temperature interval causes simultaneous decomposition of the precursors.
The brief high-temperature interval causes near-random incorporation of the constituent elements.
Rapid cooling kinetically freezes the elements into a disordered solid solution before diffusion can cause phase separation or segregation.
The initial material is a uniformly mixed precursor containing more than five noble-metal salts or single-source precursors on a substrate.
Increasing high-temperature dwell time or reducing heating rate while holding peak temperature fixed increases the time available for atomic diffusion.
The proposed regime applies to systems containing at least five elements in equimolar or near-equimolar proportions.
The relevant rapid-processing range is millisecond-to-second heating, peak temperatures of approximately 1100–2000 K, and cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
Rapid thermal processing creates stochastic mixing.
The short high-temperature window freezes the elements into a metastable disordered phase.
Extending dwell time or reducing heating rate increases atomic mobility.
The increased atomic mobility permits thermodynamically driven elemental segregation, phase separation, or formation of secondary ordered phases.
The rapid-processing baseline produces homogeneous, single-phase, disordered solid-solution nanoparticles.
Longer dwell time or slower heating will produce detectable segregation, secondary phases, and potentially altered particle morphology relative to the rapid-processing baseline.
Large differences in precursor redox properties or decomposition temperatures can impede simultaneous precursor conversion and may place a composition outside the proposed regime.
Substrates that substantially alter heat transfer may place the synthesis outside the proposed regime.
The dwell-time or heating-rate threshold for transition from a single phase to phase separation is not defined and may depend on the elemental combination.
Failure of increased dwell time or reduced heating rate to cause any detectable segregation, phase separation, or crystal-structure change would falsify the suppressed-mobility hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis, initial state, and boundary require more than five elements, whereas the conditions state at least five elements, inconsistently including exactly five-element systems.
